Research Program

Research

My research integrates plant physiology, agronomy, and horticulture to address crop production challenges in California agriculture, with particular emphasis on vegetable systems and related work in grapevine and other woody perennial crops.

The program focuses on how crops respond to water, nutrient, and disease related stress, and on how physiological understanding can inform management under field conditions.

Current work is centered on leafy greens, especially lettuce, and combines field, greenhouse, and laboratory approaches. The broader emphasis is on research that is rigorous, relevant to California agriculture, and useful to both academic and industry audiences.

Research Areas

Current areas of work

Vegetable crop stress physiology

Research on how vegetable crops respond to environmental and physiological stress, with emphasis on leafy greens in California production systems.

Irrigation and nutrient management

Applied work on irrigation and nutrient management practices that improve crop performance, resource use, and resilience under field conditions.

Plant hydraulics and water relations

Basic and applied research on water transport, hydraulic function, and plant responses to drought and irrigation.

Plant anatomy, imaging, and crop health

Work linking plant structure, imaging approaches, and physiology to crop health, disease response, and stress tolerance.

Sensor based crop monitoring

Use of sensing, imaging, and quantitative tools to assess plant status and support crop monitoring and management.

Approach

The program combines field, greenhouse, and laboratory research, including plant physiological measurements, structural imaging, and sensor based approaches to crop monitoring.
